item.subject: science
item.chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
item.stem: Meera's grandmother follows a purely lunar calendar in which each month begins with a new Moon, and 12 such lunar months make one lunar year of about 354 days. Meera notices that a festival fixed to a particular lunar month falls in winter one year but, after several years, falls in the rainy season. Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.A: The Moon's phases change randomly, so no calendar based on them can ever repeat in a regular way.
options.B: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar year ends earlier and the months drift through the seasons.
options.C: The seasons themselves become a little shorter each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
options.D: The Moon takes exactly 30 days to complete its phases, which matches the seasonal year, so any mismatch must be due to counting errors.
